title: Musk Is Now Worth a Trillion Dollars. SpaceX Hit $2 Trillion on Day One. India Still Will Not Let It Turn On Starlink.
excerpt: The largest IPO in history minted the world's first trillionaire. For India, the most relevant SpaceX product remains stuck in regulatory limbo.
body:
Elon Musk rang the opening bell from Starbase, Texas, on Friday morning. By the time most Indians were finishing dinner, he was worth more than a trillion dollars.

SpaceX shares opened at $150 on the Nasdaq, jumped 19 per cent through the day, and closed at $160.95 — giving the company a market value of $2.1 trillion. It is now the sixth-most-valuable company in the United States, larger than Broadcom, larger than Tesla, and closing in on Amazon. The $75 billion IPO was the largest in history, eclipsing Saudi Aramco's 2019 debut.

Musk, who owns roughly 85 per cent of SpaceX's voting power, is now worth an estimated $1.1 trillion according to Forbes. No human being has ever been worth this much. The milestone was met with celebration at Starbase and Times Square, protest outside JPMorgan's headquarters in Manhattan, and a giant Musk effigy in front of the Nasdaq building the day before.

**What SpaceX actually is in 2026**

The company that went public on Friday is not just a rocket maker. In February 2026, SpaceX absorbed Musk's AI startup xAI, gaining the Grok chatbot and the social network X. Starlink, the satellite internet arm with more than 5 million subscribers across 100-plus countries, remains the only profitable division. The rest — reusable rockets, the Starship programme, orbital data centres, Mars colonisation — bleeds money. SpaceX disclosed an accumulated deficit of $41.3 billion since its founding in 2002 and lost $8.7 billion between January 2025 and March 2026.

Investors do not seem to care. More than 510 million shares worth $84 billion changed hands on the first day — a smoother debut than Meta's glitch-ridden 2012 listing. Analysts at Goldman Sachs, which served as lead bookrunner, say the total addressable market for SpaceX's combined businesses is $28.5 trillion.

**India is still keeping Starlink out**

For the 1.4 billion people in India, the most immediate product SpaceX could offer is Starlink. High-speed satellite internet could transform connectivity in rural India, where terrestrial broadband barely reaches. But India has not granted Starlink a licence to operate.

The standoff is about spectrum allocation, security clearances and pricing. India's Department of Telecommunications has insisted that satellite spectrum be allocated administratively rather than auctioned — a position that favours incumbents like Reliance Jio's satellite venture. Musk has made no secret of his frustration. Indian regulators have made no secret of their caution.

With SpaceX now a $2 trillion public company, the commercial pressure to crack the Indian market — the world's second-largest by mobile subscribers — will only intensify. But the regulatory timeline remains unclear, and India's domestic telecom lobby, led by Reliance and Bharti Airtel (which backs rival satellite operator OneWeb), has every reason to slow Starlink's entry.

**What it means for Indian tech**

The SpaceX IPO does not exist in isolation. It is part of a wave of AI-adjacent mega-listings, with Anthropic and OpenAI waiting in the wings. For India's $315 billion IT services sector — already reeling from a 27 per cent drop in the IT index this year and a $62.8 billion market cap wipeout in February after Anthropic launched its AI agent tools — the message is uncomfortable.

The companies that command the highest valuations in 2026 are not services firms. They are infrastructure plays: rockets, satellites, chips, AI models. India has deep engineering talent but no SpaceX, no Nvidia, no Anthropic. The "picks and shovels" opportunity that Lighthouse Canton and BlackRock have identified — data centres, cooling systems, power infrastructure — is real but incremental.

Musk himself, from Starbase, offered the pitch that has made him the world's richest person. "Not just a few astronauts," he said. "I mean literally you. Whoever you are watching this, SpaceX wants to be able to take you to the moon, take you to Mars and ultimately beyond."

For now, it cannot even take Indians online.
